title: equals, hashCode and toString

notes: toString makes println show (4, 5) instead of Spot@1b6d3586.
== compares identity: two `new` objects are never ==.
equals compares meaning: same x and same y.
hashCode uses the same fields as equals, so HashMap finds the key.
@Override makes the compiler check you really replaced Object's method.

exercises.title: Readable crops
exercises.prompt: Add toString to both classes. A Crop prints as "maize (40 kg)". A Harvest(String farmer, List<Crop> crops) prints as "Amina: [maize (40 kg), beans (12 kg)]". Hint: a List's own toString already calls toString on each item.

tests.call: new Harvest("Amina", java.util.List.of(new Crop("maize", 40), new Crop("beans", 12)))

hints: @Override public String toString() { return ...; } in each class.
Crop: name + " (" + kg + " kg)". Harvest: farmer + ": " + crops

exercises.title: Grid points as keys
exercises.prompt: Point(int x, int y) is a square on a game map. Override equals (same x and y; false for null or for anything that isn't a Point) and hashCode (Objects.hash), so points work in a HashSet and as HashMap keys. toString is done.

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { java.util.HashSet<Point> s = new java.util.HashSet<>(); s.add(new Point(1, 1)); s.add(new Point(1, 1)); s.add(new Point(2, 1)); return s.size() + ""; }).get()
tests.name: HashSet removes duplicates
tests.hint_if_fail: A HashSet needs both equals and hashCode.

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { java.util.HashMap<Point, String> m = new java.util.HashMap<>(); m.put(new Point(4, 5), "chest"); return m.get(new Point(4, 5)); }).get()
tests.name: HashMap lookup
null
tests.hint_if_fail: o instanceof Point is false for null: check it first.

hints: The parameter must be Object: public boolean equals(Object o).
if (!(o instanceof Point)) return false; then cast: Point p = (Point) o;
public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }

exercises.title: Medicine stock tally
exercises.prompt: Medicine(String name, int mg). equals is already written: names match ignoring capitals, and mg must match. But hashCode is missing, so a HashSet counts "Paracetamol 500" and "paracetamol 500" twice. Add a hashCode that agrees with equals. Then write static Map<Medicine, Integer> tally(List<Medicine> meds) that counts how many times each medicine appears (use a HashMap). distinct() is already written.

tests.call: Medicine.distinct(java.util.List.of(new Medicine("Paracetamol", 500), new Medicine("paracetamol", 500), new Medicine("Paracetamol", 250)))
tests.name: distinct

tests.call: Medicine.tally(java.util.List.of(new Medicine("Amoxicillin", 250), new Medicine("AMOXICILLIN", 250), new Medicine("ORS", 1))).get(new Medicine("amoxicillin", 250))
tests.name: tally

hints: equals ignores case, so hashCode must too: hash the lowercased name.
tally: counts.put(m, counts.getOrDefault(m, 0) + 1); for each medicine.

choices: true only if equals is overridden
quiz.why: == on objects compares identity; these are two different objects.

quiz.q: You override equals but not hashCode, then add two equal points to a HashSet. Most likely size?
quiz.why: Different default hashes put them in different buckets, so equals is never asked.

quiz.q: Which header really overrides Object's equals?
quiz.why: The parameter must be Object; equals(Point) is just an overload.

quiz.q: equals compares names ignoring case. What should hashCode use?
quiz.why: Equal objects must have equal hashes, so normalise the same way.

choices: Printing and debugging show useful text
quiz.why: The default ClassName@hash tells you nothing.

cards.a: == : same object. equals: same meaning (if overridden).
Objects.hash(field1, field2) using the fields equals uses.
The compiler checks you really override it (catches equals(Point)).

explain: Explain why HashMap needs both equals and hashCode, using a game map or a medicine shelf as your example.
